title: Déisi
extract: In early medieval Ireland, the Déisi (Irish: Déisi, meaning 'vassals' or 'subject peoples') were a social class rather than a single ethnic group. The term referred to autonomous but tributary peoples who had been displaced from their original territories and resettled in new regions. The most prominent of the Déisi kindreds were the Déisi Muman ('Déisi of Munster'), who gave their name to the modern counties of Waterford and South Tipperary. According to the Expulsion of the Déisi, the Déisi Muman were expelled from Leinster and resettled in Munster as vassals of the Eóganachta dynasty of Cashel. The Déisi Tuisceart ('Northern Déisi') became the ancestors of the Dál gCais, the dynasty of Brian Boru. According to the Historia Brittonum, the Uí Liatháin and a 'significant force of the Déisi' colonized Wales, Cornwall, and Devon in the post-Roman period, and were driven out of North Wales by Cunedda and his sons. The surname Deacy derives from the Irish Uí Dhéisigh, a sept of the Déisi Muman resettled in south Connacht.
